snippet.title: The Female KGB Agent Who Stole America's First Atomic Bomb Blueprint | True Cold War Story
snippet.description:
In the summer of 1945, a 32-year-old seamstress from the Bronx walked out of Albuquerque, New Mexico, carrying the implosion lens design of the Fat Man atomic bomb — hidden inside a cardboard box of Kleenex tissues. Her name was Lona Cohen. Her Soviet intelligence codename was LESLIE. Four years later, the Soviet Union detonated its first atomic bomb. This is the documented story of why.

The complete investigative history of the most consequential act of atomic espionage in Cold War history — from the Manhattan Project laboratories at Los Alamos to a nondescript bungalow in suburban London. From the NKVD recruitment of two Bronx communists in the 1930s to the collapse of the Portland Spy Ring in January 1961. Built entirely from primary sources: declassified Venona Project transcripts, Soviet archival records, and NSA intelligence files.

Theodore Hall, the youngest physicist at Los Alamos, voluntarily handed the Soviet Union the implosion lens blueprints of the Fat Man plutonium bomb at nineteen years old. Klaus Fuchs provided the theoretical framework from inside the British scientific mission. David Greenglass fed the Rosenberg spy network from the machine shops. And Lona Cohen — a former seamstress with no scientific training — walked out of New Mexico with all of it in a Kleenex box and boarded a passenger train east.

snippet.title: How Coca Cola Helped FBI Catch a Soviet Spy (Cold War Story)
snippet.description:
In the late 1970s, a quiet bookstore in Arlington, Virginia displayed a single Coca Cola bottle in its front window. Most people never noticed it. For one FBI agent, the bottle became an anomaly he could not ignore. It appeared at irregular hours, always placed with an unusual deliberateness, and always followed by small changes inside the shop that no one else seemed to see.

As investigators watched from a distance, they uncovered a pattern hidden in plain sight. The bottle was not decoration. It was a signal, part of a quiet routine linking a Pentagon employee to a Soviet handler. Over weeks of surveillance, early morning stakeouts, and patient observation, the ordinary became suspicious, and the suspicious slowly revealed the outline of a covert exchange moving through an unsuspecting neighborhood.

This dramatized story reflects how fragile normal life could be during the Cold War. A single object, something familiar and harmless, could carry the weight of betrayal. And in this case, it became the first clue in an investigation that exposed a spy operating where no one expected him to be.

snippet.title: How FBI Caught a Soviet Spy inside a Walmart (Cold War Story)
snippet.description:
In 1989, the final years of the Cold War were unfolding quietly, and for nearly a decade, a man known as Michael Vernon lived an ordinary American life. He rented a modest apartment, worked for defense contractors, shopped for groceries, and blended seamlessly into suburbia. But he wasn’t who he claimed to be. His real name was Viktor Chernov. A Soviet intelligence officer planted deep inside the United States.

The FBI launched an operation to find him and flush him out. After years of surveillance, missed leads, and quiet suspicion, they finally closed in.
The arrest didn’t happen on a dark street or in a secret facility, it happened at a Walmart in plain sight.

This story recreates the final hours of Chernov’s cover, the moment ordinary life and Cold War espionage collided under fluorescent lights, and the uneasy truth that the world’s most dangerous secrets often hide in the most mundane places.

snippet.title: How Chaos Shaped the 1920s: Hyperinflation, Revolutions and New Powers
snippet.description:
Discover how the world unraveled and rebuilt after World War I - from hyperinflation in Germany to the rise of fascism, and the chaos that shaped the 1920s economy.

This video dives deep into the turbulent aftermath of World War I, examining the economic collapse, political revolutions, and social upheavals that defined the early 1920s. Explore the consequences of the Treaty of Versailles, the failed attempts at peace, and the fragile international agreements like the Washington Naval Conference. Learn how Germany’s hyperinflation devastated everyday life, leading to shocking scenes like wheelbarrows of worthless banknotes and the infamous rise of Adolf Hitler. We also follow the collapse and recovery in Austria, the surge of fascism under Mussolini in Italy, and the economic struggles that paved the way for dictatorships across Europe and beyond.

The video also explores the global ripple effects: Japan’s recovery and devastation from the Great Kanto earthquake, America’s roaring 1920s, the revival of the Ku Klux Klan, and the birth of mass consumer culture with cars, radios, and movies. Witness how France, Britain, and the United States responded to the world’s economic instability, and how key treaties and plans like the Dawes Plan and Treaty of Locarno attempted to stabilize Europe. We track the rise of totalitarianism in Russia under Stalin, colonial tensions in Syria and China, and the explosive growth of extremist groups in Germany. Throughout, the narrative connects the dots between economic hardship, social unrest, and the political forces that would ultimately lead the world towards another global conflict.

snippet.title: The KGB Defector Who Walked Out of His CIA Handlers in a Restaurant | True Cold War Story
snippet.description:
In 1985, senior KGB defector Vitaly Yurchenko walked into the American Embassy in Rome and handed the CIA two of the most damaging intelligence traitors in U.S. history. Ninety-three days later, he walked out of a Georgetown restaurant — and drove straight to the Soviet Embassy.

This is the fully documented story of Vitaly Yurchenko — the highest-ranking KGB officer ever to defect to the United States, and the only Cold War defector who ever came back.

During three months of CIA debriefing, Yurchenko exposed two Americans who had been selling classified secrets to Soviet intelligence:

→ Edward Lee Howard — a CIA case officer who became the only CIA officer in history to defect to the Soviet Union. He fled to Moscow before he could be arrested. He died there in 2002, age 51, under unexplained circumstances.

→ Ronald Pelton — an NSA analyst who sold the KGB the secrets of Operation Ivy Bells, the covert program that placed listening devices on Soviet undersea military communications cables in the Sea of Okhotsk. Pelton was convicted and spent 30 years in federal prison.

Both identifications were real. Both produced consequences that lasted decades.

Then, on the evening of November 2nd, 1985, Yurchenko walked out of Au Pied de Cochon on Wisconsin Avenue in Georgetown, flagged a taxi, and disappeared. Three days later he held a press conference at the Soviet Embassy in Washington — claiming the CIA had kidnapped and drugged him in Rome. The CIA denied everything.

The real reason he walked out has never been established.

Was Yurchenko a genuine defector — broken by a devastating personal rejection in Ottawa by a woman he had traveled far to see? Or was he a KGB plant from day one, sent to identify CIA officers, map American intelligence procedures, and come home with everything he had learned?

Four decades later, the question is still open.

snippet.title: January 28th, 1945: The Day That Marked the Beginning of the End of WW2 | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
January 28, 1945. One hundred days remain until Germany surrenders. The Red Army is advancing with 3,800 tanks and 1.5 million soldiers, and almost half a million German soldiers have already died in this month alone. The war is no longer a question of whether Germany will fall, but how many more will die before it does. These final hundred days are the most savage, chaotic, and devastating of the entire conflict. A refugee ship carrying 10,000 people sinks in the freezing Baltic. Dresden burns for days. Berlin is bombed in daylight by a thousand aircraft. Millions of civilians flee eastward across frozen lakes with Soviet tanks on their heels. And in the Reich Chancellery, Hitler and Eva Braun have already quietly decided they will not survive it. This is the story of the hundred days that ended the Third Reich, told through the eyes of those who lived and died inside them.

snippet.title: The Soviet Spy Living Next Door Who Almost Got Away With It (True Cold War Story)
snippet.description:
For 19 years, a KGB-trained Soviet spy lived in suburban America under a stolen identity — raising an American family, working at MetLife, attending school events — while nobody suspected a thing. The FBI identified him in 1988 and watched him in silence for 9 more years. His name was Jack Barsky. He was never prosecuted. He is alive today.
This is the fully documented Cold War story of Albrecht Dittrich — a KGB illegal intelligence officer recruited at Friedrich Schiller University in East Germany, given the stolen identity of a dead American child, and dispatched into the United States in October 1978 with no diplomatic cover and no protection. If discovered, there was no embassy to call. Only federal charges and a sentence measured in decades.
What the KGB did not plan for was simpler and more human than any intelligence failure: a daughter born in New York, a country that surprised him, and a decision in 1984 — when Moscow ordered him home — to stay. He told the KGB he had AIDS. He did not. He used the only craft he had left to buy himself the life he had stopped pretending to live and started actually living.
The FBI found him anyway. What they did with him — and why — is one of the most unusual outcomes in American counterintelligence history.

snippet.title: The CIA Operative Who Spent 9 Years Living a Lie Inside Moscow | True Cold War Story
snippet.description:
In 1977, CIA officer Martha Peterson became the first woman to run a clandestine intelligence operation inside Soviet Moscow — and when the KGB finally caught her on the Krasnoluzhsky Bridge, it took a full ambush team to stop her. Their own field report initially listed her as male.
This is the fully documented story of TRIGON — one of the CIA's most productive Cold War intelligence operations inside the Soviet government, dismantled by KGB counterintelligence, and ended by a cyanide capsule hidden inside a pen.
Martha Peterson arrived in Moscow in October 1975 under diplomatic cover, assigned to handle a Soviet intelligence asset codenamed TRIGON: Aleksandr Dmitrievich Ogorodnik, a Soviet Foreign Ministry official recruited by the CIA in Bogotá, Colombia in 1974. Ogorodnik had access to classified Soviet Foreign Ministry cables — the internal diplomatic correspondence of Soviet foreign policy as it was actually decided — and provided the CIA with intelligence assessed among the most valuable human intelligence the United States held from inside the Soviet government during that period.
For nearly two years, Peterson ran a series of Moscow dead drops embedded in public parks, river embankments, and residential streets. Concealment devices disguised as rocks, tree branches, and asphalt fragments were loaded by Ogorodnik and retrieved by Peterson through counter-surveillance routes that could last two to three hours each. The KGB monitored every foreign diplomat in Moscow. Neither Peterson nor Ogorodnik made a single operational error.
What brought the operation down was patient counterintelligence analysis. The KGB's Second Chief Directorate detected an anomaly: American negotiating positions in several multilateral forums appeared calibrated to nuances visible only in classified Soviet Ministry of Foreign Affairs documents. Working backwards through the Ministry's document distribution, the KGB identified Ogorodnik and positioned an ambush team at the bridge before Peterson arrived on July 15th, 1977.
Peterson was expelled from the Soviet Union on July 20th, 1977. Ogorodnik was arrested days later. At Lefortovo Prison, he asked for a pen to write a confession — the same pen the CIA had provided in Bogotá three years earlier, with a cyanide capsule concealed inside its barrel at his own request. He died in the interrogation room. He was thirty-seven or thirty-eight years old.
In 2012, Martha Peterson published The Widow Spy, the only firsthand account of the TRIGON operation.

Ogorodnik had access to classified Soviet Foreign Ministry cables — the internal diplomatic correspondence of Soviet foreign policy as it was actually decided — and provided the CIA with intelligence assessed among the most valuable human intelligence the United States held from inside the Soviet government during that period.
For nearly two years, Peterson ran a series of Moscow dead drops embedded in public parks, river embankments, and residential streets. Concealment devices disguised as rocks, tree branches, and asphalt fragments were loaded by Ogorodnik and retrieved by Peterson through counter-surveillance routes that could last two to three hours each. The KGB monitored every foreign diplomat in Moscow. Neither Peterson nor Ogorodnik made a single operational error.
What brought the operation down was patient counterintelligence analysis. The KGB's Second Chief Directorate detected an anomaly: American negotiating positions in several multilateral forums appeared calibrated to nuances visible only in classified Soviet Ministry of Foreign Affairs documents. Working backwards through the Ministry's document distribution, the KGB identified Ogorodnik and positioned an ambush team at the bridge before Peterson arrived on July 15th, 1977.
Peterson was expelled from the Soviet Union on July 20th, 1977. Ogorodnik was arrested days later. At Lefortovo Prison, he asked for a pen to write a confession — the same pen the CIA had provided in Bogotá three years earlier, with a cyanide capsule concealed inside its barrel at his own request. He died in the interrogation room. He was thirty-seven or thirty-eight years old.
In 2012, Martha Peterson published The Widow Spy, the only firsthand account of the TRIGON operation.

snippet.title: "Find The Limp" — The Tiny Detail That Caught A Soviet Spy In Mexico City
snippet.description:
On September 27, 1963, CIA surveillance cameras photographed a young man entering the Soviet Embassy in Mexico City. Six weeks later, that man—Lee Harvey Oswald—would assassinate President John F. Kennedy. But the CIA didn't identify him from those photographs until after the assassination. This is the story of how one analyst's meticulous attention to physical detail finally connected the surveillance images to Oswald's identity, and why that identification came too late to prevent a national tragedy.

🔍 THE MEXICO CITY SURVEILLANCE OPERATION

In 1963, the CIA's Mexico City station ran Operation LILYRIC—continuous photographic and audio surveillance of Soviet and Cuban embassies. Station Chief Win Scott oversaw cameras that automatically photographed everyone entering or exiting the compounds, generating hundreds of images daily. The volume was enormous. Most photographs sat in files, analyzed only when subjects were identified as intelligence officers or known operatives.

Lee Harvey Oswald wasn't considered high-priority. His file showed he was a former Marine who had defected to the Soviet Union in 1959, lived in Minsk, married a Russian woman named Marina, and returned to the United States in 1962. But nothing suggested he posed an imminent threat.

🇲🇽 OSWALD IN MEXICO CITY

From September 27 to October 2, 1963, Oswald visited both the Cuban and Soviet embassies repeatedly, seeking visas to return to the Soviet Union. He became increasingly agitated as officials told him the process would take months. Soviet KGB officers who met with him later described him as mentally unstable and desperate. His visa applications were denied.

CIA cameras captured him entering and exiting the Soviet Embassy multiple times. Audio surveillance recorded his telephone calls. But in the routine workflow, these materials weren't immediately analyzed in depth. Then came a critical error: photographs of a different man were mistakenly associated with Oswald's name in CIA cables to headquarters. This misidentification would persist for six weeks.

🔫 NOVEMBER 22, 1963

Oswald returned to Dallas on October 3rd. He rented a room under the alias O.H. Lee and obtained employment at the Texas School Book Depository on October 15th—a building overlooking Dealey Plaza. On November 22nd, as President Kennedy's motorcade passed below, Oswald fired three shots from a sixth-floor window. Kennedy died at Parkland Hospital at 1:00 PM. Oswald was arrested that afternoon and killed by Jack Ruby two days later.

🕵️ THE URGENT REVIEW

After the assassination, the CIA launched an intensive review of all Mexico City surveillance materials. The misidentified photographs clearly didn't show Oswald—wrong age, wrong height, wrong appearance. Where were the actual photographs?

Ann Goodpasture, a photo analyst who had worked at the Mexico City station since 1957, began systematically reviewing every image from late September. She compared surveillance photographs against post-arrest images of Oswald, examining facial features, body type, clothing, and physical characteristics.

According to accounts of the analysis that emerged later, the identification involved comparing multiple observable details. Oswald had accidentally shot himself in the left elbow during Marine Corps service in 1957, resulting in permanent nerve damage that affected his posture—his left shoulder sat slightly lower than his right, creating a subtle asymmetry visible to careful observers.

Goodpasture's analysis, reviewing the totality of physical characteristics visible in the surveillance photographs, concluded with reasonable confidence that the September 27th images showed Lee Harvey Oswald. A cable correcting the earlier error was sent to CIA headquarters.

⚖️ THE WARREN COMMISSION

The Warren Commission investigated whether Oswald's Mexico City contacts indicated foreign involvement in the assassination. Soviet and Cuban officials consistently denied any connection. Declassified documents supported their accounts. The Commission concluded Oswald acted alone, motivated by personal and ideological factors rather than foreign direction.

But critical questions remained: If the CIA had identified Oswald from surveillance photographs before the assassination, would he have been flagged for FBI monitoring? Would closer surveillance have prevented the tragedy?

Intelligence officers acknowledged the inherent limitations: massive volumes of collected material, finite analytical resources, and the impossibility of predicting which individuals among thousands photographed would prove significant.

Jefferson Morley, "Our Man in Mexico" (2008)
John Newman, "Oswald and the CIA" (2008)
Declassified CIA Mexico City Station files

For 43 Years Britain Hid What Happened in Its Own Waters

From nineteen sixty-one to nineteen ninety-two, the United States Navy operated a nuclear submarine base at Holy Loch in Scotland — without a parliamentary vote, without Scottish consent, and without telling the public what happened there in November nineteen seventy-four. A Soviet Victor-class submarine entered British territorial waters and came dangerously close to an American nuclear-armed ballistic missile submarine. Both governments suppressed it for forty-three years. Based on declassified British and American documents.

snippet.title: 250 Years Later: Why Everything You Learned About the American Revolution is Wrong
snippet.description:
Forget what you learned in school. Or from Hamilton. The American revolution was bigger and bloodier than you ever thought.

For the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, we bring you the undiscovered stories, heroes, and villains of the War for Independence. In this incredible six-part retelling, we go far beyond the 13 original colonies and the clash between American Patriots and British colonial troops. We traverse the Atlantic and plunge deep into the American West to discover a multi-front war that engulfed a diverse cast of characters – Indigenous people, enslaved Africans, American Loyalists, women of all social classes – and changed the face of world history.

EPISODE 4: A POOR MAN’S FIGHT
We tell the story of one of the first large battles in Manhattan and kips bay as this newly formed army struggles to fight the world’s largest empire 

EPISODE 5: REMEMBER THE LADIES
As men march off to war, a number of women make their case to be heard and included.  We tell the story of Abigail Adams, the feminist wife of John Adams, who writes a series of radical letters, advocating for improved conditions and political rights for women. 

EPISODE 6: A NEW WORLD
The final episode examines how the final years of the Revolution shaped Britain and the global balance of power as the United States enters the game of empires.
